e.t: This word means “arm,” referring to the limb extending from the shoulder and used in ordinary bodily description. It is a noun, so it names the body part rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Job 24:19. The available lexical definition establishes its basic meaning, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain any particular figurative or contextual force.

Atharin is a proper name, referring to a person or place identified by that name in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here with an additional descriptive meaning or translated concept. Atharin occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Numbers 21:1. Because the surrounding verse text is not included, the name’s specific role in that passage cannot be explained further from this word entry alone.

This word means “sensitive,” describing someone or something capable of feeling or perceiving impressions. As a noun, it points to sensitivity itself or to a sensitive quality rather than naming a specific action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Proverbs 14, including Proverbs 14:10 and Proverbs 14:30. Its precise force in either saying depends on the surrounding verse and how sensitivity is being discussed there.

This Greek LXX adverb means “suddenly,” describing something that happens unexpectedly or without warning. It tells the reader how an action or event occurs, rather than naming the action itself. The word appears twice in the LXX corpus, both times in 2 Maccabees, at 2 Maccabees 5:5 and 14:22. Its basic sense remains focused on abruptness: something takes place quickly and unexpectedly.

This adjective describes someone who is “speechless; dumb”—unable to express words aloud. It refers to a lack of speech rather than naming a person or action. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs twice, both times in Psalms, so its basic meaning is clear but its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage. It is used in Psalms 30:19 and 37:14.

This word means "milking": the act or process of obtaining milk. It is a noun, naming the activity rather than a person, animal, or tool. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 20:17. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise role in that sentence depends on the passage itself; its basic meaning remains the act of milking.

Amoth is a proper name, referring to a specific person or place rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears only once, in Joshua 19:14, and is rendered “Amoth.” The available information identifies the name itself but does not provide the surrounding verse text, so its precise referent in that passage must be determined from the context of Joshua 19. As a name, Amoth functions as a distinct designation rather than a word with a broader everyday definition.

This noun means “in exchange”: something offered or received in place of something else. It expresses the idea of a trade, repayment, or substitute, depending on the sentence where it appears. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times across nine verses, including passages from Ruth, Kings, Job, Psalms, Jeremiah, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being exchanged and the surrounding words.

This adjective describes something that cannot be successfully resisted: it is “not to be withstood” or “irresistible.” It can characterize a force, action, or power that opposition cannot overcome. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures represented here, the word occurs three times, so its central sense is consistent but its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

gl: make rise up and depart; send away
d: make rise up and depart; send away

e.t: This verb means to make someone rise up and depart, or to send someone away. It describes movement away from a place or the act of causing another person to leave. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 1:5; the surrounding verse text is not available here, so the word’s precise force in that sentence depends on its context. Its central idea remains removal or departure. This is a Greek LXX word, distinct from Greek New Testament vocabulary.

This adjective describes something “not to be filled” or “insatiate”—a condition that remains unsatisfied rather than becoming full. It can describe a person, desire, or appetite that does not reach satisfaction, depending on the surrounding verse. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, the word occurs five times, chiefly in Proverbs, with one occurrence each in Psalms and Sirach. Its precise emphasis in any verse comes from the thing or desire it describes.

This verb means “have enjoyment of”: it describes experiencing something as pleasing or satisfying. It focuses on the enjoyment received from something, rather than merely possessing or encountering it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, keeping this central idea consistent across its uses. The surrounding verse identifies what is enjoyed, while the word itself expresses the act of enjoying it.

Aran is a proper name, referring to a person named Aran rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it appears nine times, including passages in Numbers, Deuteronomy, Kings, Chronicles, Jeremiah, and Baruch. Because it functions as a personal name, its meaning is primarily its identifying reference: Aran is the individual designated by that name in each passage. The surrounding verse is needed to identify which Aran is intended and what role that person has there.

This word means “lamb,” the ordinary name for this animal. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings to identify a lamb when one or more are mentioned. It occurs 16 times in this LXX corpus: 14 times in Old Testament books and twice in deuterocanonical writings. Thus its basic sense is straightforward and concrete, while the surrounding passage determines what is being said about the lamb.

This word means “asp,” referring to a venomous snake. It is a noun used for the creature itself rather than for an action or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 29 times across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, including passages in Deuteronomy, Psalms, Job, and Isaiah. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the asp as a dangerous snake.

This adjective describes something indecent—behavior or a situation regarded as improper or dishonorable. In the Greek LXX, it appears four times across Genesis, Deuteronomy, Wisdom, and 2 Maccabees. Its basic force is negative: it marks conduct or circumstances that fail to meet a proper standard of decency. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being called indecent, but the word itself consistently points to something shameful or unsuitable rather than acceptable.

gl: with bad grace; with an ill will
d: with bad grace; with an ill will

e.t: This Greek adverb means acting “with bad grace” or “with an ill will.” It describes the manner in which someone does something, emphasizing an unwilling, resentful, or begrudging attitude rather than willing kindness. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 18:18. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wider context, but its central meaning points to an action performed without good will or gracious readiness.

This word is a proper name presented as “Baithōrōn” or “Vethoron.” It identifies a named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 17 times, from Joshua through 1 Maccabees. Its repeated appearance in geographical and historical passages shows that it functions as a fixed name, while the surrounding verse is needed to identify its specific role in each occurrence.

This Greek LXX verb means “exalt” or “make proud”: it describes raising someone up in honor, status, or inward confidence. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person or thing. It occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Numbers 23:24, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic sense remains the act of exalting or making proud.

This word means “ring,” naming a circular object or ornament. It is a noun used for both a single ring and more than one ring, depending on the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 39 times, with many occurrences in Exodus and additional uses in Genesis, Esther, Daniel, and Bel and the Dragon. Its normal meaning remains the physical object called a ring.

Dekla, also known as Thekla, is a proper name—the personal name of an individual. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, at Genesis 10:27. The name itself identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not part of this entry, the name’s specific role in that passage cannot be stated here.

This word is a personal name, rendered “Dēsōn” or “Thison,” rather than a term describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times in six verses: four times in Genesis and twice in 1 Chronicles. Its appearances are concentrated in Genesis 36 and 1 Chronicles 1, where it functions as an identifying name. The name itself does not provide a broader vocabulary meaning beyond identifying the person named.

This Greek verb means “threaten violently.” It describes speech or action intended to intimidate someone through forceful threats, rather than a gentle warning or ordinary statement of danger. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented by this LXX entity, it occurs three times, including once in Ezekiel and twice in 3 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a severe, intimidating threat.

This verb means “give” or “deposit”: to transfer something to another person, place, or purpose. It can describe providing a gift, handing something over, or entrusting something for safekeeping or later use. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs 1,890 times, showing that giving and handing over are frequent actions in its scriptural vocabulary.

This verb means “build across” or “wall off,” describing the act of constructing something that spans or closes a space. It is a practical building word, focused on putting up a barrier or structure rather than merely planning one. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 2:17. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains the construction of a structure across an opening or the enclosing of an area.

This word is a noun for a deed or act—something done. It names an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it appears once, at 4 Maccabees 6:17. The word’s basic meaning is therefore straightforward: it refers to a deed or act, while the surrounding verse determines exactly which action is meant there.

Edeia is a proper name, also represented as Ethia. It functions as a personal designation rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 22:1. The available wording identifies the name but does not provide its personal meaning or explain the individual’s role. Its significance in that verse therefore depends on the surrounding passage and the person being named.

This Greek LXX verb means “melt out” or “destroy.” It describes an action in which something is caused to dissolve, waste away, or be brought to ruin. The wording can therefore express the removal or breaking down of something rather than merely observing its condition. It occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, including Leviticus, Job, Psalms, and Sirach. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun refers to refuting or reproving—the act of directly challenging or correcting what is wrong. It names an act rather than a person, place, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 19 times across 18 verses, appearing in books such as Leviticus, Numbers, Psalms, 2 Kings, Sirach, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any sentence depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains a clear act of refuting or reproving.

Elisama is a proper name used for people in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or object; it identifies a person by name. The name occurs 15 times in the Greek LXX, across 15 verses, including passages in Numbers, Samuel, Chronicles, and Jeremiah. Because it is a personal name, its exact significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and the person being identified there.

This Greek LXX adverb means “crosswise.” It describes how something is positioned or done, indicating a direction or arrangement across rather than along a straight line. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Genesis 48:14. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, its precise force in that passage must be understood from the sentence itself. Its basic meaning remains a description of something arranged or performed crosswise.

This Greek LXX verb means “send forth” or “discharge.” It describes an action in which someone or something is released, sent out, or dismissed from a place or situation. As a verb, it expresses what a person does rather than naming an object or quality. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 12:24; the surrounding verse is needed to determine its precise force there.

This verb means to “pay in full” or “spend.” It describes the act of using or disbursing something until the required payment has been completely made. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 12:13, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated biblical examples. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the thing being paid or spent.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a cover or a heave-offering. It can name a covering object, or an offering set apart and presented in worship. The wording allows both senses, so the surrounding passage determines which one is intended. It occurs 19 times in the Greek Old Testament, especially in passages concerning the tabernacle, priestly portions, offerings, and sacred observances.

This noun means an “object of desire”—something a person longs for or strongly wants. It can refer to a desired thing rather than to the feeling of desire itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it occurs 16 times, showing use across descriptions of valued possessions, hoped-for things, and what people earnestly seek. The precise force in any passage depends on what is being desired and the surrounding sentence. Its central idea remains a thing that attracts longing or is regarded as especially desirable.

This verb means to remember or to call something to mind again. It describes bringing a person, matter, or past event back into one’s thoughts. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Maccabees 10:46, so its broader range cannot be established from repeated uses here. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included in this entry.

This adjective means “delightful.” It describes a person, thing, or circumstance as pleasing in character or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, both times in the book of Wisdom: Wisdom 4:10 and Wisdom 9:10. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains a positive description of what is delightful.

This adjective describes something that has been boiled or prepared, especially food. It identifies the condition of an item after cooking or dressing rather than naming an action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Numbers 6:19 and 1 Samuel 2:15. The precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic sense remains a prepared or cooked item.

This noun means “hegemonides.” The supplied lexical meaning preserves the word as a title or designation, but no further English definition is available. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Maccabees 13:24. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the specific person or referent cannot be identified from the word alone. Its exact force in that passage therefore depends on how the surrounding sentence uses this noun.

This verb means “sprout”: to begin growing or to put forth new growth. It describes the emergence of a plant or something pictured as coming up and developing. The word appears five times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this LXX corpus, including Genesis, Job, Proverbs, and Sirach. Its central idea is fresh growth becoming visible, whether used for a plant itself or as a comparison. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is sprouting, but the word consistently points to the beginning or visible expression of growth.

This word is a proper name, referring to “Thesbōn; Thezvon.” In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Kings 17:1. The name itself identifies the subject designated by the passage, but the available lexical information does not establish whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity. Its precise significance in that verse must therefore be understood from the surrounding biblical text.

This noun means a store or treasure: something kept as a valuable reserve or possession. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 21:6. Its basic sense points to accumulated wealth or valuables rather than to the act of gathering them. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly how this word functions in that passage, but its normal meaning is a stored treasure or valuable store.

Iakareēl, also rendered Iakaril, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Joshua 15:38. The available information identifies its name-form and location in the text, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain whether it names a person, place, or another specific entity. Its precise referent therefore depends on the context of Joshua 15:38.

Iōarim, also written Ioarim, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 9:10. Because the available information identifies the name but does not provide the verse text or surrounding passage, its specific identity and role must be understood from that passage’s context. The name itself is preserved as a proper name, not translated into an ordinary English meaning.

This adverb means “badly” or “ill,” describing the manner in which something is done or the poor condition in which someone is found. It can therefore point to harmful, unsuccessful, or unhealthy circumstances, depending on the sentence around it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 15 times, appearing in both Old Testament books and deuterocanonical books. Its exact force in any particular verse comes from the action or condition it describes.

Karapha, also given as Karafa, is a proper name in the Greek Septuagint. It identifies a named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs once in the LXX, at Joshua 18:24. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the available information does not establish whether Karapha refers to a person, place, or another named entity. Its precise significance therefore depends on reading that passage in context.

This Greek LXX verb means to abide or dwell—to remain in a place or continue there. It describes staying rather than merely arriving or passing through. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times, including passages in Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, and Bel and the Dragon. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls on living somewhere, remaining there, or continuing in a given situation.

This Greek LXX verb means “burst into flame”: it describes something suddenly catching fire or blazing up. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in Psalm 17:9. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage, but its basic meaning is a sudden outbreak of flame or burning.

This noun refers to wages—the cost paid for labor or work. It describes compensation connected with someone’s effort, rather than the work itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in the books of Exodus and Deuteronomy. Its basic sense remains focused on the payment or expense associated with labor, while the surrounding verse determines the specific situation being described.

This Greek LXX verb means “inherit”: to receive something as an heir, especially property, land, or a designated share. It describes the act of coming into an inheritance rather than merely possessing something temporarily. The word occurs 153 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing a repeated connection with receiving an allotted possession. In passages about people, families, or nations, its basic sense remains receiving what is assigned or passed down as an inheritance.

This noun means a “hunt” or “chase”—the pursuit of someone or something. It names the activity itself rather than describing the person who hunts or the one being pursued. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Sirach 13:19, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic sense remains the pursuit involved in hunting or chasing, whether understood as a literal activity or as language used by comparison.

This verb means “render speechless”: to cause someone to become unable to speak. It describes an action or effect rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs twice, both in Psalm 38, showing a focused use in this corpus rather than a widely repeated term. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains causing speechlessness. The word is found in Psalm 38:3 and Psalm 38:10.

This word is a proper name rendered “Libanos” or “Livanos.” It identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures, rather than describing an action, quality, or ordinary object. The name occurs 97 times in the LXX corpus, across 89 verses, with occurrences from Exodus through Song of Songs. Its exact reference in any particular verse must be understood from that verse’s surrounding context.

This verb means “weaken through hunger.” It describes the effect of lacking food: a person becomes physically weakened because of hunger. The word functions as a verb, expressing an action or process rather than naming hunger itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Deuteronomy 8:3. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the weakening caused by hunger.

Maacha, also written Maakha, is a proper name identifying people in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a common word describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs 11 times across 11 Old Testament verses, from 2 Samuel through 2 Chronicles. Because the same name can identify different people, the surrounding verse is needed to determine which Maacha is meant in a particular passage. Its basic meaning is therefore the personal name "Maacha; Maakha," rather than a broader concept or title.

Malecheth, also rendered Malekheth, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 7:18, identifying a particular person or name in that genealogical record. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, the name’s specific identity and role cannot be described more precisely. Its normal meaning in this corpus is therefore the personal name Malecheth or Malekheth.

Marimōth is a proper name, rendered “Marimoth,” used to identify a named referent in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or object; it functions as a name. This name occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Ezekiel, at Ezekiel 47:19 and 48:28. The surrounding verse text is needed to identify the named referent in each passage.

Machathi, also rendered Makhathi, is a proper personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, in 2 Kings 25:23 and 1 Chronicles 4:19. The available information identifies the name itself but does not provide a separate meaning or explanation of its possible name origin. Its significance in either passage must therefore be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

This verb means “divide”: to separate something into distinct portions or parts. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Job 40:30, so its exact force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic idea is the act of splitting or distributing rather than keeping something together as one whole. The word is therefore an action word, describing what someone or something does when portions are separated or assigned.

Mephaath, also rendered Mefaath, is a proper name for a place. It is not a descriptive word or an action; it identifies a named location in the Greek Old Testament. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Joshua 13:18. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself establishes the place designation but does not provide further detail about the location or its significance.

This adjective means “only” or “alone,” describing someone or something without others alongside it, or identifying one thing as the sole one. It can therefore express either singleness—being by oneself—or exclusivity—being the one and not another. In the Greek Old Testament represented by this LXX word, it occurs 131 times, so it is used broadly for both situations. The surrounding sentence determines whether the emphasis is on isolation or on being the sole person or thing in view.

This Greek LXX verb means “ridiculed”—to treat someone with scorn or make them the object of mockery. It describes an action rather than a person or thing, so it tells what someone did to another. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, in Jeremiah 28:18. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, which are not included here; but its basic meaning remains clear: someone was ridiculed or mocked.

Naphek, also written Nafek, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named person or place in the Old Testament passages where it appears, but the available lexical information does not specify which. This name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, in Exodus 6:21 and 2 Samuel 5:15–16. Its precise reference in each passage must be determined from the surrounding verse and passage.

Netouphat is a proper name, also given as Netufat. It is not presented here as an ordinary descriptive word, but as the name of a specific person, place, or group named in the passage. This Greek LXX entity occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 27:13. Without the verse text and surrounding context, its precise referent cannot be identified further; the supported meaning is simply the proper name Netouphat or Netufat.

gl: attempt anything new; make a violent
d: attempt anything new; make a violent

e.t: This verb means to attempt something new and can also describe making a violent or forceful move. It expresses active, bold action rather than simply thinking about a possibility. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 3:21. Its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense points to trying something unfamiliar or acting forcefully.

This noun means “mistress of the house,” referring to a woman who holds the household’s domestic position or authority. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Exodus, Leviticus, and Proverbs. The word identifies a household role rather than naming a general category of women. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation.

This noun refers to a “whole burnt offering,” a sacrifice presented as a complete offering. It can also be rendered “sacrifice,” but its central idea is an offering given wholly rather than only in part. The word appears four times in the Greek Old Testament and Wisdom, including passages in Leviticus, Numbers, and Wisdom. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies a complete sacrificial offering.

This verb means “dig.” It describes the action of breaking into or removing earth, usually to make an opening in the ground. As a verb, it tells what someone does rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 31 times, with repeated appearances in Genesis and other Old Testament books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the physical act of digging.

This word means “discipline”: instruction or correction intended to shape a person’s conduct. As a noun, it refers to the guidance, training, or correction by which someone learns wisdom and proper behavior. It is a broad term in the Greek LXX corpus, occurring 137 times across the represented Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its precise emphasis in a particular passage depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains formative discipline rather than mere punishment.

This Greek LXX noun means “preparation”: the act or process of getting something ready. It refers to readiness arranged before an undertaking, rather than to the undertaking itself. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 15:21. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise role in that sentence must be understood from the passage itself. Its central idea remains the making of needed arrangements or becoming ready for what is about to happen.

This Greek LXX noun means “patriarch,” referring to a recognized father or ancestor of a family line. It is used as a title for an important ancestral figure rather than as a general word for any man. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, including passages in Chronicles and 4 Maccabees. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means “tie” or “fasten”: it describes securing something by attaching it firmly. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek text represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 3:7. The lexical sense is clear, while the precise object being fastened and the force of the action must be understood from that verse’s surrounding text.

This Greek LXX verb means to constrain or contain—to hold something within limits, surround it, or keep it from moving beyond a boundary. It can describe a force, space, or condition that presses in or encompasses something. The word occurs 33 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic idea is used across both physical and figurative settings. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being held or enclosed.

This Greek verb means “fall”: to move downward from a higher or standing position, or to come down suddenly. It can describe a person or thing falling, and its precise force depends on the surrounding sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs 375 times, showing that it is a broadly used word for falling or coming down. The word appears throughout these writings, from Genesis through the Epistle of Jeremiah.

This noun means “long journey,” referring to an extended trip or passage from one place to another. It presents travel as lengthy rather than brief, but the word itself does not explain why the journey was made or what happened during it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 57:10. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage, which give the journey its particular context.

This adjective means “costly”: it describes something that carries great expense or value. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Scriptures represented by this LXX corpus, it is used 13 times for things regarded as precious or requiring substantial cost. The word can describe material possessions, offerings, or things valued more highly than ordinary goods. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word means “recently”. It is an adverb that places an action, event, or statement near the present in time. It points to something that happened not long ago, rather than in the distant past. In the Greek LXX material, this word appears once, at 3 Maccabees 1:19. The reference identifies where it occurs, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain the particular situation in which it is used.

Raseph is a proper name, rendered “Raseph” or “Rhasef.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, the name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 7:25. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its specific family connection or role cannot be stated safely. The name itself carries no broader lexical idea beyond identifying the person associated with it in that genealogical record.

Saraph is a personal name, rendered as “Saraph” in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 4:22. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, the name itself does not establish the person’s character, role, or significance; those details must come from the context in which the individual is mentioned.

This noun means a covering or veil—something that covers or partly conceals. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, all in the Song of Songs, and each occurrence is rendered “veil.” The word therefore names a visible covering rather than an action or quality. Its precise significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a veil or covering.

This verb means “steady; steadfast.” It describes making something firm, stable, or securely established, and can also express the condition of being held firmly. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, it occurs 52 times, showing a broad use for establishing or sustaining people and things. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains firmness rather than uncertainty or instability.

This verb means “get acquainted with”: it describes becoming acquainted with or having dealings with someone. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs only twice, both in Genesis, so its basic sense is clear but its exact force in either passage must be understood from the surrounding verse. It is a verb rather than a noun, naming an action or interaction rather than a permanent relationship or specific action by itself.

This verb means “gather”: to bring people or things together, or to assemble in one place. It is a normal action word in the Greek Old Testament, describing collection or assembly rather than a particular object or group. The word occurs 345 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing broad use across these writings. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being gathered and the surrounding passage.

This verb means to “send off together,” describing the act of dispatching two or more people as a group. It focuses on sending them jointly rather than separately. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Exodus 33, so its recorded use is limited to that chapter. The precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains a combined sending or commissioning.

This noun means “fencing with ropes,” referring to the measured marking or enclosing of land by rope boundaries. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Joshua 17:5. The word therefore describes a practical boundary-making process rather than a person, object, or abstract quality. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is the division or marking of territory with ropes.

Sōphat is a proper name, rendered “Sōphat” or “Sofat,” rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named individual or figure in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 27:29. Because it functions as a name, its meaning is primarily identification: it points to the person designated by Sofat in that passage, not to a general concept used throughout Scripture.

This Greek LXX noun means “sequence,” referring to things considered in an ordered progression. It identifies an order or succession rather than an isolated item, so its role is to show how people, groups, or things stand in relation to one another within an arrangement. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, with most occurrences in Numbers, where ordered groupings are prominent. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective describes something arranged in four rows. It refers to an orderly, repeated layout rather than merely expressing the number four. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs three times, including descriptions connected with the priestly breastpiece and a sacred object. The word points to the way something is set out or organized: four distinct rows placed in an ordered arrangement. The exact objects and significance belong to their surrounding passages, but the word itself supplies this clear visual description.

This noun means “self-indulgence”: a life centered on excessive pleasure, comfort, or luxury rather than restraint. It describes an attitude or way of living, not merely a single enjoyable experience. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 25 times, showing that the word is used across wisdom, prophetic, and other biblical writings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains the pursuit or enjoyment of excessive ease and pleasure.

This noun means “belonging,” referring to what is connected with or possessed by someone or something. It identifies an association or possession rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 13 times, including passages in Chronicles, Ezra, Psalms, Proverbs, Jeremiah, and the Maccabean books. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what the surrounding sentence identifies as belonging and to whom or what it belongs.

This Greek LXX verb means “endure” or “stay behind.” It describes continuing through difficulty or remaining when others may leave, rather than giving up or moving away. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 78 times, so it is used broadly for steadfast continuation. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what or whom the person is enduring, and whether the emphasis is persistence, waiting, or remaining in place.

gl: look at from below; view with suspicion
d: look at from below; view with suspicion

e.t: This verb means to look at someone from below or to view that person with suspicion. It describes a guarded, distrustful way of observing rather than a neutral glance. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, in 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. The surrounding verse wording is needed to determine what prompted the suspicious look in either passage, but the central sense remains an attitude of wary observation.

Pharphar, also rendered Farfar, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or abstract idea. It identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament translation. This name occurs once in the LXX, at 2 Kings 5:12. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, its precise role in that passage cannot be described further; the supported lexical meaning is simply the name Pharphar or Farfar.

This word means “murder,” referring to the unlawful taking of a person’s life. It is a noun, so it names the violent act rather than describing someone who performs it. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it appears 21 times, showing repeated use for serious bloodshed and violent killing. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains murder. [p03:word:lxx:L713549:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L713549:occurrences]

This Greek LXX noun means “copper; brass,” referring to a reddish or yellow metal used as a material. It names the metal itself rather than an action, person, or quality. The word occurs 57 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, so it can describe metal in a range of passages without changing its basic meaning. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding text, but the central idea remains copper or brass.

Chanana, also rendered Khanana, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person named Chanana. This name occurs five times, in five verses, across 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, and 2 Chronicles. Its precise significance as a personal name is not defined by the available passages, so it is best understood simply as the name Chanana or Khanana.

This word means “pallium,” a noun naming a garment or outer covering. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 31:22. The word identifies a clothing item rather than a person, action, or quality. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains a pallium: a garment referred to by name. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that corpus.

This noun means “soul.” It names the soul rather than an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs 900 times across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so it is a broadly used biblical word rather than a rare or specialized term. The available English rendering also gives “soul,” matching this basic meaning. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This noun means “elegance” or “adornment”—something that gives beauty, attractiveness, or a pleasing appearance. It can describe outward beauty or the way something is made appealing. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Jeremiah 4:30, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic sense remains the quality or decoration that makes someone or something appear beautiful or attractive.
